entries.title: A Two-Person Startup Has Fixed One of the Most Hated Sounds in Modern Life
entries.content:
I behave very strangely in my kitchen. On any given day, you will find me, often mid-conversation, sprinting from one end of the room to the other. Nothing on the stove has caught fire. No pots are boiling over. I am trying to reach the microwave oven before its counter hits zero.

Why? I detest so deeply its shrill beep heralding the completion of its reheating duties that it's almost as if the appliance has trained me, through operant conditioning, to open its door at T-minus 1 second, so the grating noise is silenced before it begins. But there is another way, a means by which microwave makers can keep their margins, not change the hardware in any way, and, just by manipulating a few lines of code, change the kitchen experience sonically for the better for aurally assaulted microwavers everywhere.

Enter Joel Corelitz and Colin Coogan from Starling, sound designers who have previously worked with clients including Sony, Microsoft, Netflix, and Sega, as well as on major projects such as a sonic strategy for Ford's entire lineup. Corelitz, much like the rest of us, loathes his microwave's unbearable beeps, so he decided to see if they could do something about it.

Beep Beep

The beep has cursed humanity for a relatively short period of time. The use of “beep” to mean a short, high-pitched sound first appeared in an Arthur C. Clarke sci-fi story, The Sands of Mars, as recently as 1951. Before this, “beep” was used as a descriptor of the sound of car horns.

For decades now, nearly all microwaves have used the same technology to generate their penetrating pings: a small, cheap device called a passive piezoelectric buzzer. It's a membrane that, when electrically charged, vibrates, producing a rudimentary beep.

The piezo buzzer was first brought to the mass market in the 1970s by Japanese manufacturers. Thanks to their low cost—piezoelectric buzzers cost a matter of cents—and simplicity, the buzzers soon found their way into all manner of gadgets: toys, smoke detectors, alarm clocks, multimeters, watches, and, yes, microwaves. However, the versatility was matched by limitations. Manufacturers can set the beep's frequency and duration, but that's about it. This has not stopped the basic tech from still being widely deployed in all manner of gear.

Manufacturers can add speakers to a microwave, allowing the appliance to reproduce a cornucopia of aural delights. But the reason the vast majority of microwave manufacturers stubbornly stick with offensive beeps is, naturally, cost. Competition in consumer white goods is fierce. Why replace a super-cheap part that does the job with something pricier?

The challenge Corelitz and Coogan set themselves was this: better microwave sound, sound with some personality; but no new hardware, so using existing chips and existing buzzers. Everything had to be done just with code.

“Any microcontroller that accepts C++ can take different programming and produce different sounds," Corelitz says. "There's already a microcontroller in there, and there's already a piezo buzzer.” He has fashioned a series of sounds that are a world away from traditional microwave beeps, yet all are created using the same kit inside the box sitting in your kitchen.

On a laptop using software the pair have created called Microwave Sound Bench, Corelitz demonstrates by re-creating the horrendous beeps we know and hate. Then he switches to Starling's alternatives. Trills where the duration of notes is super short; frequency sweeps that sound like a cartoon falling object; arpeggios; a “sequence of events” that create a noise that seems like it belongs more in a video game. None sound like a microwave. All are a thousand times better than the cortisol-inducing tone that emits from my kitchen each morning.

“I'm doing it all on an Arduino, but it's really just C++," Corelitz says. "A manufacturer would have to be open to putting new code in their device, but that's it. It's theoretically compatible with any hardware that's in a microwave.”

His test-specific setup is laughably minimal: a microcontroller (the Arduino UNO R4 Minima), and a breadboard with three different piezo buzzers attached for comparing output—two attached directly to the breadboard (the black circular objects), and one bare buzzer stuck to a sheet of paper, which helps it resonate more.

Corelitz has a way to fake volume from piezo tech. “If you sweep through the frequencies, you'll notice that at a certain frequency range the buzzers just sound louder, because they prefer that resonance,” he says. “You can use that resonant frequency to simulate dynamics.” And it works. You'd swear Starling's sounds get louder and quieter, but that's not happening.

To banish repetitive harsh beeps when pressing multiple buttons, like when you're cycling through the microwave's menus, Starling has also re-created the soft, premium click you get on your smartphone when typing. “I just wanted to see what a 4,000-Hz beep for one millisecond would sound like, and I was like, ‘Oh, that actually sounds pretty good.’ It would make a microwave infinitely more satisfying to use,” Corelitz says.

Coogan says it can be more challenging to communicate a lot with a little, which made the challenge more enticing to them both. But the response on Instagram seems to suggest there's more than sound aesthetics at stake here.

“One of the top things that people kept commenting over and over again was, ‘Oh my God, I would pay $50 more for a microwave that sounded better,’” Coogan says. It seems there's gold in them thar trills.

Sound Design

Richard Hughes, now Volvo's design lead for digital user experiences and interfaces in North America, was the principal UX designer at Whirlpool for 15 years. He knows his beeps. He also knows why established brands still sell bad-sounding microwaves.

“A lot of these companies don't have internal audio expertise," Hughes says. "They do on engineering for product noise, but very little sound design.”

Hughes, while at Whirlpool, did indeed experiment with beeps in a remarkably similar way to Starling, using piezos hooked up to an Arduino. And he says the company launched a KitchenAid Pro Line toaster where people loved its piezo sound.

“It was a very expensive toaster, but people referenced its ‘flight attendant call button’ sound,” Hughes says. “It was a much softer, rounder sound, and people love that to this day.” No such care went into fettling microwave audio at Whirlpool, according to Hughes, because the company just didn't produce a premium model where users would expect better beeps. Many of the microwave's sounds are carried over from one product to the next.

“[Manufacturers] may update the aesthetic, but the technical insides, that behavior spec is carried over, which is why they all sound the same, they all sound awful, and it's that piercing noise we've all come to hate.”

Fortunately, it seems we're finally about to enter a world where our microwave sounds don't suck. “It's trickling down," Hughes says. "Companies have been focusing on product lines with more margin, but you're going to see that cascading into the microwave.” He added that when he finished at Whirlpool, he led a sound strategy initiative for a few products that should be entering the market right about now. As part of those strategies, Hughes made it imperative that Whirlpool assess what the lowest common denominator looked like at the piezo level.

This is, after all, the very definition of low-hanging fruit. An easy win. No extra hardware cost, just attention to detail. “Within the last few years, realization has hit that ‘delighters’ play a key role in someone purchasing your product," says Hughes. "The things that make it a little more magical.”

The duo at Starling agree. That's what they aim to supply: delighters. And since putting their sonic experiments out there, while they'd be delighted to work with the likes of Panasonic or Samsung, they're not concerned if a company wants to “borrow” their ideas and take things in-house.

“It's not a big fear that someone's going to steal this," Corelitz says. "I'd hope our sensibilities as designers, as audio consultants, is more valuable than this. We just want to solve the problem of going through the world hearing noises that are annoying and don't contain good information.”

So, now that microwaves are sorted, what's next? Does Starling have a hit list of annoying noises? “Oh, we have a few,” Coogan says. “We'll have to see who wants to work with us.”

entries.title: Can the New York Times Save Journalism From Our AI Overlords?
entries.summary: In 2023, the Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft for copyright infringement. They’ve since spent more than $20 million on the case, and publisher A.G. Sulzberger has no plans to stop fighting it.
entries.content:
For most companies, spending upwards of $20 million on a single legal fight with an uncertain outcome might mean the boss has some explaining to do. For A.G. Sulzberger, the publisher of The New York Times, that explanation is simple: It’s the cost of defending journalism—at the Times and everywhere else.

Sulzberger, who took on the publisher role about a decade ago and has been an influential leader in the Times’ much-lauded push into digital innovation, has no shortage of defending to do lately. Nearly three years ago, the Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft for copyright infringement, alleging that the companies illegally used New York Times journalism to train AI models. That legal case, in which motions are still being filed about discovery requests, is only one front in a broader battle: The Trump administration is waging an ongoing war on press freedoms—most recently with an outrageous attempt to subpoena Times journalists over coverage of the president’s Qatar-gifted jet to be used as Air Force One—while AI companies radically reshape the way people find and consume information online.

The Times has arguably never been stronger as a business, having recently surpassed 13 million subscribers, and its newsroom is widely seen among journalists as one of the most stable and well-resourced in the business. Still, Sulzberger believes that journalism itself is facing myriad existential dilemmas—from an administration ready and willing to target reporters, from AI companies whose products depend on the very reporting they risk undermining, and media companies being demolished by the changes they’re unleashing on the open web.

I sat down with Sulzberger in late July at WIRED’s offices. We talked about that Times lawsuit, how and where AI is transforming reporting inside the newsroom, and why he thinks journalists and media executives need to team up—even while they continue to compete fiercely. You can read our entire conversation below, or listen to it here.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

KATIE DRUMMOND: AG, welcome. Thank you for being here.

A.G. SULZBERGER: It's great to be here. Thanks for inviting me.

I want to get into AI, and I will, but I would be a terrible journalist if I didn't start with news that has recently affected your paper.

Specifically, I'm talking about the subpoenas that the Justice Department has issued to several Times journalists about their reporting on the Air Force One jet that was gifted to the Trump administration by Qatar. The Justice Department also issued subpoenas to third-party phone service providers to obtain text messages and phone calls between some of those journalists and their family members.

Thanks for starting there, because it’s obviously yet another disturbing escalation in the Trump administration's efforts to punish and undermine the free press in this country.

First I should say, I have so much admiration for the reporters who have done this work and who are doing it under a different kind of pressure than we have seen in generations. I think that by any objective metric, this is the biggest effort to go after the press that we've seen from a White House probably since Woodrow Wilson, so in more than a century.

These reporters just continued, day after day, to put their heads down, right? Not to get baited by the folks booing them or the folks cheering them on, and just to do their work. That work includes reporting things that the President of the United States doesn't want the public to know because it may be unflattering or embarrassing.

In this case, they reported a story, as you said, on the Qatari-donated jet, and it's a little unclear: Was it donated to the Trump administration or to Trump himself? A donation worth hundreds of millions of dollars.

Right.

When that occurred, a lot of people had questions about whether it could ever be secure enough to hold the President of the United States and ferry him around the world. Sure enough, our reporters found out that on one of its inaugural trips, its first trip overseas to Turkey, there were concerns that it was insufficiently equipped to respond to a threat, that the president had to fly back on the original Air Force One. He denied this initially. But we exposed the truth, which has subsequently been confirmed.

Then it gets even stranger.

Every administration, we will publish something that the President of the United States doesn't want the American people to know. Upsetting a president of either party is nothing new to us. What is new is that the administration defied many of its own standards and practices and explicit guidelines to very rapidly, in the course of a day or two, serve subpoenas on these reporters. They went straight to the homes of reporters, in an obvious attempt to intimidate them. As you said, we are now learning that they sought to get records, not just from the reporters themselves, but from members of their families. It's a gross overreach.

Just to contextualize for listeners, how unusual is all of that? To have law enforcement at your home as a journalist, to be subpoenaed right out of the gate, to have those phone records called up by the Justice Department. How weird is that?

I mean, it's extremely unusual. It's very rare. The closest comparison that I have had at the Times in my tenure—I've been in this job roughly a decade—happened in the first Trump administration, when some of our reporter records were secretly seized by the Justice Department. In fact, that led to some reforms in the Justice Department aimed at curtailing that type of abuse.

On one side this is objectively very rare—there was similar overreach, you may remember, in a Washington Post case some months ago, where they actually raided the reporter's home and seized her devices—[but] on the other [hand], this is building naturally off of what I think is a broader effort.

You have also criticized other media outlets for capitulating to the administration, particularly around settling what you've called winnable cases to appease Trump. Do you still see your peers as largely capitulating?

I don't think I ever said largely capitulating. I actually think that the industry has largely held its ground. And to be very clear, holding your ground does not mean an adversarial posture. It means being willing to publish the truth even when powerful people get angry at you for publishing it.

It means being willing to ask any question, no matter who it might upset. I actually think that the industry, by and large, has done very good work. WIRED’s done good work. The [Wall Street] Journal has done terrific work. The Associated Press. When the White House conditioned their continued access to the White House on them switching from calling a big body of water the Gulf of America instead of the Gulf of Mexico, they didn’t take that sitting down.

I remember this.

They sued, and I think rightly. They sued regardless of whether they win the case, right?

Right.

One of the things that I'm saying to peers in the industry regularly is that your rights only hold if you seek to enforce them.

You may not win every battle, but the surest way to lose your rights is to avert your eyes, drop your head, and try to avoid notice and just take what comes.

I do think that some news organizations have clearly felt the pressure from the administration and I think allowed that pressure to affect coverage.

My colleagues in Washington tell me that they're regularly talking to reporters at other news organizations who are saying that they will no longer pursue certain stories, because they're too worried that their editors will kill them because of fear of retaliation, and that their model is actually to wait for an institution like the Times to report the story, and then they'll follow it, and they think that that's a fight they can win. But breaking the story, being the one to first upset the White House, seems like a road too far.

That is the definition of chilling, right? That's when the message that retaliation and punishment must be avoided gets down to the lowest levels of the newsroom. Now, my job as publisher of the Times is to make sure the opposite message is getting through, right?

After these great reporters were served these subpoenas, I called each of them and I said, “We have your back, and we'll do whatever we need to support you.” One of the things that I was most encouraged to hear in those conversations, although not surprised, these are tough guys, was that they said, “Oh, we're not gonna let go of this story.”

Good. As a journalist myself, and I run a publication that takes heat here and there, I worry sometimes about how we better translate that to the audience. So making sure the public understands how essential this work is, and exposing them to the work itself, especially in the context of AI. How do you think about that? What else can news organizations be doing to make sure that audiences are exposed to the work and see and understand the value of the work, and what it means when that work stops happening?

Look, I agree that we haven't done good enough of a job as an industry on that. We've sort of taken it for granted. At the Times I think about just the outsize investment we are making on behalf of the public's right to know. We put reporters on the ground in 150 countries last year. Every year, over 150 countries. Last year, we had reporters on the ground in Myanmar, in Sudan, in Lebanon, in Iran, in Venezuela, in Gaza, in Israel, in Russia.

In Ukraine alone, we had more than 70 journalists on the ground. And I am sure, although we've never done it, that if we dug in, it's really hard to find the financial case for those expenditures.

Yes. I would agree with you there.

I am sure, though I've never done it, that when I look at all the investigative reporting we've done, and this is reporting that takes months, sometimes years of work to produce a single story, that it would be very hard to justify all those expenditures, right?

But I think the public sometimes doesn't know how much institutions like ours think about the civic good. I really believe, as our Founding Fathers did, and across all their lines of division, the Founding Fathers agreed that a free people need a free press and that a country that aimed to steer itself needed access to independent and reliable information.

Jefferson famously said, given the choice between a government without a press or a press without the government, he wouldn't hesitate to choose the press. And that's because this work really does matter to society.

Journalism is quite simply very often how you know what you know. Shifting over to AI, it's how AI knows what it knows.

Yes, let's get into that. In the context of AI in journalism, I break it into two buckets. For WIRED, there's reporting on this technological moment in time, which is really important. And then there's the separate question, although we cover that as well, of how AI will affect the practice of journalism and the consumption of journalism.

I mean, there are really difficult lines to walk here, and I'm curious about how you think about that at The Times.

I think my philosophy is you very rarely in life need to be first. There is a risk of jumping too quickly into an emerging technology. And there's probably more risk in that than waiting, watching, learning, studying, experimenting quietly behind the scenes. I think you saw some of those risks, right? Like, think about the news organizations that, in my mind incredibly foolishly, decided to just hand over full responsibility for writing and publishing articles to AI. Mistakes were made.

Mistakes were made. And mistakes were published.

That is right. And not just mistakes were published, but fake journalists were invented. It was a completely foreseeable and unnecessary set of mistakes. Humans are responsible for everything we produce, period. And there's something about AI that has tricked people into forgetting that it is a tool.

Well, it's a very good conversation partner.

But when my colleagues say, "Well, what if AI makes a mistake?" I say, "Well, then it’s your job to find that mistake and take it out of your work." You would never ask that about a computer. What if a computer makes a mistake?

Well, you gotta find it, right? I view this as a reporting tool. So we're using it much more in reporting than writing, crafting, editing.

I think AI is very good at spotting patterns and anomalies in large data sets. In many ways, that's a pretty good summation of a big part of reporting. You know, campaign finance reporting is basically what are the patterns, how is the mix of donors to the Republicans and Democrats changing, big donors for small donors, and then anomalies.

One of the reporters who won our first Pulitzer that involved AI-supported reporting, what he said to me is, "You have to think of AI as a filter.”

In his case, he was examining bomb craters in the Israel-Gaza conflict, and he said that it regularly makes a certain kind of mistake. So the way to think about AI is it took millions of images and it shrunk it down to thousands of images. But it was his job as a journalist to look at every one of those thousands of images to make sure he felt confident in the findings.

So that's the type of experiment we're doing, and I think between that natural posture of, we wanna take our time and move with curiosity and creativity, but also some degree of care and caution, and that we as journalists, as reporters, as editors, are ultimately responsible for the work.

I think that's how we've avoided most mistakes.

I agree with you. I think it is a very valuable tool, or can be used to create very valuable tools, for reporting and for reporters, especially as newsrooms have gotten smaller. I think there's a competitive advantage there. I will say at WIRED we are building our own AI tools for reporting, and one of the goals is actually to beat The New York Times more often. So we're trying to get clever in ways that maybe other news organizations aren't when it comes to using AI.

Everyone needs competition. So we'll watch with interest.

But in a speech recently, you also said there are early signs to be concerned about when it comes to how AI will affect fact-based reporting. I mean, some of those are obvious. But talk to me about what you see as those early signs. What worries you most here?

It's really important just to go back to what I referred to in that speech as the original sin of AI.

There are four ingredients in good AI products: There are the people who write the code; there is what we call compute, the chips and data centers, et cetera; there is electricity; and there is what Silicon Valley calls data but which is content, journalism, books, music, movies.

And let's just go through those four right now. On the coders, you literally have contracts that are sports-star level.

Oh, they're paid like NBA players. It's outrageous.

Hundreds of millions of dollars for a single individual coder at times. Now let's look at compute and electricity. Literally, these companies are taking hundreds of billions of dollars of debt in order to pay for those things. That's how big the prize is if they win. These are companies that all now have trillion-dollar valuations or near-trillion-dollar valuations, right? So the prize is big.

Now you get to data, and they've just taken it. They've just taken it all. Without permission and without any compensation, because they thought they could. They think they can get away with it. And if they can get away with that, then that boosts the profit margins of the richest and most valuable companies in the history of humanity. And if the casualty is that it completely guts what remains of our already financially beleaguered industry of journalism, so be it.

If it completely undermines the financial models for professions like book writing and music making and movies and TV and academic research, then so be it.

That is objectively the wrong thing to do. It is also not allowed under US law. Protections for what is called intellectual property date back all the way to the Constitution, so it is not legal to come in and take all this work.

Why does this all matter? Why do I feel some degree of alarm about this? You know it has already been challenging to compete with the giant platforms that basically exercise a monopoly over human attention, right?

That's a little overstated, but if you added up all the minutes of a day, a handful of platforms and a handful of companies occupy the vast majority of those, right? But now you're not just competing with companies that are controlling the vast majority of human attention, right? Companies that are actually designed to be maximally intermediating. Companies that feel that AI will work best if it sits in between the user and the content creator.

Google is one sort of really salient example here.

It's hard to overstate the degree to which publishers relied on traffic from Google referral links and the degree to which that traffic has disappeared in the last year, year-and-a-half, as Google has introduced AI. So now when you search, you get an AI Overview.

It's reasonably helpful, usually helpful enough that you don't need to click through. Even just that change has been crushing.

And you are suing, you are in a years-long lawsuit. You said recently you've spent, what, $20 million on this legal battle against several big AI companies for copyright infringement. How is that suit going, if I may ask?

And I'm curious, what is your ideal outcome from that lawsuit, not just for The New York Times but for the news industry more broadly. What do you hope to accomplish there?

Let me first just linger on the number you just said. We are two and a half years into this lawsuit. Two and a half years. And we have spent well over $20 million on this lawsuit, and we are not yet through discovery.

I didn't realize that. Wow.

Yeah. So when you think about this original sin, this theft of every creative work ever created, it amounts to this immense wealth transfer, right? From creators and researchers around the world to the biggest tech companies in the history of humanity. That sense of impunity that they can just take our stuff is happening in part because of how expensive it is to enforce your rights. The Times, thankfully, we've worked really hard to put ourselves in a financial position where we can enforce our rights.

Can you imagine being a small-town newspaper and being able to take on Google or OpenAI or Microsoft or Perplexity.

I mean, it's not gonna happen.

It's impossible. It's just completely unfeasible. So these companies have been backed into this awful position, where AI companies have already stolen your stuff. They say explicitly they're going to use it regardless, and then sometimes they'll throw a little bit of money your way. What do you do? Do you try to spend what may end up being $40 million on a lawsuit? Or do you accept the pennies on every dollar you spent to create your work just to recoup something?

We think it's really important to enforce our rights and say “absolutely not.” Like, you want to use our stuff, that requires permission, and that requires fair compensation.

Someone needs to fight that fight. Thankfully, we're not the only ones filing a lawsuit like this. A number of other publishers in the industry have filed similar lawsuits.

Our parent company has a few.

Silicon Valley has tried to portray our lawsuit as anti-tech.

They have.

It is not anti-tech. It is anti-theft, and anytime you hear the anti-tech line, I just want you to picture Jensen Huang coming down onto the floor of his Nvidia factory, discovering that Sam Altman has snuck in and has arms full of chips and he's running out of the building.

What a visual.

And Jensen says, "Hey, you're not allowed to take that." And Sam Altman says, "If you tell me that I can't take this, you're anti-tech, Jensen. You're gonna make China win."

We are not anti-tech. We are anti-theft. This is not about money. This is about the ability to sustain essential work.

You've talked a few times about our profession, journalists and news executives, linking hands on this issue of AI. Teaming up to get ahead of it, to win. What does it look like to you to compete and team up at the same time? Because we all compete fiercely.

Well, who would you say was the closest, fiercest competitor of The New York Times if you look at the last half century? The Washington Post.

I was thinking it in my head, trying to be emotionally generous. But that is the answer.

The Washington Post was our fiercest competitor. And boy are they fierce.

And to their credit, they still are.

To this day, there are so many good journalists at The Washington Post, and not a week goes by without them publishing something that I'm just salivating with envy over them having gotten first. So they were our fiercest competitors. They were also our closest ally when our industry came under pressure.

Just think about the Pentagon Papers. The New York Times starts publishing the Pentagon Papers. The Nixon White House goes to war with The Times. It is so dark. The threats are intensifying so much that my grandfather, who was publisher at the time, has his entire legal team quit over his decision to publish the stories, and they tell him he may spend the rest of his life in jail.

And he starts carrying a toothbrush in his pocket, in case he's hauled off at any moment.

The fresh breath was really important?

Fresh breath was really important to him in prison. So we publish the stories, we defy the Nixon White House, and eventually we will win the legal case that establishes the right that the government cannot establish what's called prior restraint, keep you from publishing something in advance.

We will end up winning that legal right. But there's a period in which we are locked down. When the court has ordered us to halt publication. And what happens the next day? The Washington Post picks up where we left off. And I could give you a dozen of those stories.

Our journalists were all kicked out of China in retaliation for some of the actions of the first Trump administration. Who was my first call? It was Fred Ryan at The Washington Post. And my second call was Will Lewis at The Wall Street Journal, and we decided that we would raise concerns about these actions collectively.

Let's compete on the stories all day long. Let's compete for the best journalists all day long. And then when our rights are attacked—the same rights that protect me are the rights that protect you and vice versa—we all come together. I think that's the posture we need in the face of these AI abuses.

There are things we can do collectively. We can tell the story of these abuses and help the public understand them. We can tell the story of journalism, what journalism is and why it matters, and the danger it faces if these abuses are allowed to continue. We can enforce our rights.

How do you win? How does our industry win? Our industry is not gonna win compared to the tech giants. We are a tiny little minnow.

Well, let’s say winning is synonymous with surviving.

And that's it. What I am worried about, and what you're worried about, and all our peers across the industry, is not about getting giant and bigger. That's what the folks in Silicon Valley are worried about. They want to take over the world. We want an essential profession, an essential service. The act of seeking the truth, helping people understand the world, holding power to account. We want that to survive, and I really believe that democracy needs it to survive.

Who else does these things if journalists don't? Is AI going to go to the front lines of the Ukraine conflict and show what's happening there? Is AI going to spend years building the sources that we need to finally get Trump's taxes and provide the fullest picture of Trump's wealth and the conflicts inherent in that.

AI can't do any of those things. And so we need journalists for it, and AI needs journalists for it. So we need to come up with a sustainable framework for all of this.

And I would argue one that ensures that The New York Times is not the only game in town. You guys need competitors.

Look, we are the first to say that.

I mean, you are a behemoth.

It's interesting that you say that we're a behemoth, and you cover behemoths here at WIRED.

You are a behemoth in the context of the news industry.

I really want to slow it down. The newsroom at The New York Times, we're really proud of it, has basically doubled the number of journalists that we have to 2,400. That is a drop in the bucket of the number of journalists that this country needs.

I could not agree more.

We’ve reached this amazing milestone. We hit 13 million subscribers. We're aiming for 15, and that sounds like a big number until you remember that Netflix is over 300 million, and you have another, you know, half dozen with a hundred, 200 million subscribers.

Actually it's all the way down the list to Crunchyroll. Crunchyroll has more subscribers than The New York Times. We are the largest player in our beleaguered industry. But what we need is the entire industry to be much bigger. If you're going to say that The New York Times is the country's leading news organization, do we really think that the country's leading news organization should have fewer subscribers than an anime streaming service?

Well, when you put it like that, A.G., I agree. What I want is for a 23-year-old journalist to look at this industry and think, "I could work there, I could work there, I could work there. Or maybe I could work there." There are not enough places to point to.

I mean, there are other success stories. I think The Journal has been doing extraordinarily well and doing great work. The Post had an amazing decade and before a couple of really tough years. The Atlantic, The New Yorker. Bloomberg may still be the largest newsroom in America.

But there aren't enough. And particularly at the local level. We've seen an 80 percent loss in the number of working journalists at the local level in this country over the last two decades.

It is completely untenable, and it is not good for anyone. One of the things that makes me appreciate Meredith [Kopit Levien] so much, she's our CEO, she's the top commercial leader of the organization, and any time she is asked, she says, “I would much rather build a market for journalism than to build a business for journalism,” like a private business.

She wants to build up that market, because the more we build up that market, the stronger we will all be. You'll have more talent in the market. You will have more competition for stories, which makes us all stronger.

It's also just really important for America. Studies show that when you lose local journalism in your community, basically every unhealthy civic metric goes up. Loneliness goes up, distrust goes up, voting goes down. Corruption goes up.

When you've got a strong local news organization, I think about Minneapolis, the Star Tribune, or The Seattle Times, the Baltimore Banner is doing amazing work. You see better civic outcomes. So I think it's important for the industry; it's important for the country.

Let me end on this, because we've talked about a bunch of really tough stuff. Crunchyroll will stay with me. What makes you optimistic? When you wake up in the morning or you're going to bed at night and you have a million things to worry about, you have a two-and-a-half-year, $20-million-plus lawsuit among them, you have the Justice Department knocking on the door of your journalists, what gives you hope and optimism for this industry?

It's a good question. This feels like a moment of great challenge, of existential challenge for our profession.

I try not to force myself to avert my eyes from that. Because you want to avert your eyes from that. But I think the AI challenge, I think the press freedom challenge, I think also the challenge of serving this incredibly polarized, tribalized public—I think of those as sort of the three great challenges of my tenure, and those are first and foremost.

At the end of the hardest days, what makes me feel like it's all worth it—and this isn't to sound corny, it's true, and you can ask my kids, because they're always complaining about it—is reading the paper. Just to remind myself, “Oh, this is what I'm fighting for.”

How to Listen

You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

entries.title: Silicon Valley’s Next IPO Billionaires Are Coming. Nonprofits Are Ready for Them
entries.summary: Anthropic and OpenAI employees are expected to give generously after their companies go public. “It’s going to be a wild ride,” says one nonprofit leader.
entries.content:
A decade ago, Ryan Carrier was a failed hedge fund manager watching as AI systems began to spin out of control. Facebook’s algorithms shook US elections, a Microsoft chatbot said the Holocaust was “made up,” and Tesla’s Autopilot killed its first driver. “There was no governance, oversight, or accountability,” Carrier says. To him, the AI-filled future awaiting his children looked bleak.

Carrier went on that year to found ForHumanity, a nonprofit organization developing tools for auditing AI systems. But it has raised just hundreds of thousands of dollars since 2016 and is still a minor player in the industry. But that could soon change, because ForHumanity is now among the many nonprofits around the world trying to rein in AI, get animals out of cages, eliminate poverty and sickness, and spread democracy that are eager to claim a slice of what’s widely anticipated to be the largest wave of philanthropy in decades.

Two nearly trillion-dollar AI companies, ChatGPT developer OpenAI and Claude creator Anthropic, are expected to go public soon, making hundreds of current and former employees ultrawealthy. Some of them are aligned with a philosophy known as effective altruism that encourages making impactful donations sooner rather than later.

Anthropic’s seven founders have pledged to donate 80 percent of their wealth, and the company has agreed to chip in one or three shares for every one its employees commit to giving, depending on when they joined and up to a certain limit.

Rough estimates by a tech industry insider suggest that Anthropic’s IPO, which could happen in September, may result in $15 billion a year in additional philanthropic giving alone. That would be enough to boost total US giving by about 2.5 percent annually—the same as adding four Bill Gates’s, one of the world’s biggest donors. Anthropic declined to comment on the total amount its employees have set aside to donate and the organizations that may benefit.

All that money is far from guaranteed. The IPOs may get delayed or go poorly and leave employees clinging onto their wealth. Industry observers are also concerned that a paralyzing number of charitable options and natural fickleness could prompt workers to keep more for themselves than anticipated.

But competition for would-be donors’ attention is already fierce. Jack Lewars, a consultant who advised 13 ultrarich tech and finance workers on their charitable giving last year, says he’s heard that employees at the AI labs are receiving as many as 20 unsolicited emails a week from groups seeking donations.

WIRED spoke with 18 nonprofits and approached dozens more to ask how they’re preparing for the potential philanthropy windfall. None of them admitted to sending cold pitches—a tactic that Lewars on his new blog, The Funding Anthropalypse, wrote “has next to no chance of working.” Instead, organizations say they are ramping up hiring, training, marketing, and use of automation to position themselves to attract massive sums of funding and quickly put it to use. One job posting at an education nonprofit even calls out building up relationships at Anthropic specifically as a priority.

“Everybody’s going to go after these funds,” says Christine Peterson, cofounder of the grantmaking group Foresight Institute, which claims to have funding from Anthropic employees. “It’s going to be a wild ride.”

The Inside Track

Like many nonprofit leaders who spoke with WIRED, ForHumanity’s Carrier says he is focusing more on the work itself than on fundraising. But he recognizes this may be a moment to shift, and he has begun wondering how to get into IPO soirees in San Francisco. “I just have to get in that room,” Carrier says.

Bo Young Lee, CEO of the nonprofit AI4ALL, says she is attending more events, putting out more research, and asking board members, such as AI scientist and entrepreneur Fei-Fei Li, to introduce her to employees at the AI labs. Her organization trains young adults across the US how to develop their own AI models, with the goal of diversifying the tech workforce. Lee says she is setting “ambitious” fundraising goals because she’s confident the money will come, though introductory meetings haven’t materialized yet.

Buck Shlegeris is the CEO of Redwood Research, a Berkeley, California-based nonprofit that is part of a growing set of small organizations pursuing what’s broadly defined as AI safety. From his perspective, targeting individual donors isn’t an optimal strategy.

Redwood has received millions of dollars from grantmaking groups such as Coefficient Giving and Survival and Flourishing Fund that pool together donations from individuals and subscribe to the effective altruism movement. Shlegeris believes that new money will flow to these intermediaries and then continue to trickle down to Redwood and others.

He says he wants to accelerate training staffers on becoming managers with the expectation that big sums of money will enable teams to grow and take on “crazy expensive projects,” like automating safety research and training Redwood’s own models. The nonprofit’s overall goal is to minimize the risk that AI could somehow lead to human extinction, which Shlegeris says he fears has a “really strong chance” of happening.

A subset of AI safety research is centered on preventing the technology from being used in the creation of bioweapons. Venture capitalist Geoff Ralston recently helped author an action plan that calls for raising $2.5 billion over the next five years to address AI biosecurity. He plans to solicit donations from those who stand to benefit from the IPO windfall. “The folks at frontier labs understand the threat vectors created by AI better than anyone,” Ralston says.

Several grantmakers influential in effective altruism circles are preparing for the giving wave by helping newer nonprofits level up their administration and bookkeeping. The goal is to ensure more organizations are ready to spend the expected influx of donations. “We’re trying to build the port before the ship arrives,” says Stien van der Ploeg, executive director at Animal Charity Evaluators, which over the past year helped direct about $15 million to nonprofits trying to reduce what they view as the worst forms of farm cruelty.

Similarly, Coefficient is making a push to support up-and-comers. This month, its largest donors, Facebook cofounder Dustin Moskovitz and his wife Cari Tuna, committed $1 billion to global health projects. It’s a “one-off surge” nearly six times bigger than initially planned but made with the intention of creating “scalable opportunities” that can “effectively absorb much higher amounts of future giving,” according to Coefficient.

GiveDirectly, another organization popular among effective altruists, says it discretely raised a round of funding from donors to support its preparations for the giving wave. The nonprofit, which transfers unconditional cash to people in poverty or crisis, is using the money to bring on more engineers to automate its finance and HR systems. It’s also forging partnerships to deploy money faster during natural disasters and has begun developing a plan for “a global AI wealth dividend” to fund people in extreme poverty. GiveDirectly CEO Nick Allardice says “despite the uncertainty” around the IPOs, it’s a moment “worth taking very seriously.”

More Cautious

Some organizations worry they'll be left behind because they're removed from the San Francisco AI community or work on issues such as child safety or political disinformation, which may not overlap with the assumed priorities of potential donors.

One broadly shared anxiety is that the sheer amount of money could leave some causes with overflowing coffers, while other urgent issues may attract little funding. For instance, groups addressing the existential risks AI poses to humanity—a priority for effective altruists—are widely predicted to receive far more backing than those trying to improve human rights by, say, fighting mass surveillance or online harms.

That possibility has been keeping Marlena Wisniak up at night. She oversees digital strategy at the European Center for Not-for-Profit Law (ECNL), which works on AI policy and research, and has been trying to raise the profile of organizations that may be overlooked, especially in the global south. This month, she scored a victory when a friend who works at Anthropic donated $100,000 to one group that fits that description. Wisniak is now trying to convince contacts at OpenAI and Anthropic to share her list of human rights and social justice organizations worth supporting with their colleagues. She is also encouraging those nonprofits to frame their work using terms like “theory of change” and “evidence-backed” that might better resonate with effective altruists.

A few organizations are deliberately sitting out the moment. Earlier this year, Model Evaluation and Threat Research, which evaluates OpenAI and Anthropic models, decided against soliciting funding from employees at those companies because it could jeopardize the nonprofit’s independence. Other groups are concerned about receiving funding from sources that would link them to effective altruism and scare away partners or other donors because the movement has been criticized as insular and misguided, according to a person familiar with the thinking of the nonprofits who sought anonymity to discuss a sensitive issue. (A communications adviser to several organizations aligned with effective altruism but not authorized to speak on their behalf says the movement “has continued to grow its funding, talent, and impact, and the increasing willingness of major funders to work with EA-aligned groups reflects that these purported reputational fears are overblown.”)

Some veterans of the nonprofit industry are urging general caution. They don't want groups to neglect their core work by contorting their projects to fit a mold appealing to the new money. It's also not lost on fundraisers that the wealth is a byproduct of building AI tools that, in some cases, are worsening the problems that nonprofits are tackling. “The risk today is this industrialized wealth from these IPOs may not serve human good in hindsight,” AI4ALL’s Lee says. “We have to avoid the allure of easy money simply to appease the prioritization of the wealthy.”

One effect of the anticipated funding surge is already emerging: As philanthropic funding concentrates in a handful of fields with limited talent pools, salaries are rising. This month, Resolution, an AI safety nonprofit, announced a $160 million grant from Coefficient, the donor’s largest award of its kind. The funding combined with the “enormous influx of philanthropic capital” following the AI IPOs will allow Resolution to pay “well above nonprofit and academic norms,” the organization said in a blog post.

entries.title: Dyson V16 Piston Animal Submarine Review: Powerful but Pricey
entries.summary: Dyson’s new stick vacuum can vacuum and mop in a single cordless device—if you’re willing to really splurge.
entries.content:
Dyson's newest headliner is here: the Dyson V16 Piston Animal, along with a Submarine version that includes a wet cleaner head. The V16 is now Dyson’s most powerful stick vacuum, unseating the Gen5Detect ($840), which held that title since 2023. This new model reports 315 air-watts (AW) of power, which is a big step up from the Gen5's 262 AW. The latest update also includes a new style of cleaner head designed for vacuuming both soft and hard floors—the All Floor Cones Sense cleaner head—which expertly tackled all floor types and debris during my testing. But is newer and more powerful always better? While the Dyson V16 is an all-around great vacuum, I’m not sold on that being the case.

With the new cleaner head, the Submarine variant for mopping, and compatibility with the docking station that's due out later this year, the V16 has better add-on options than any other vacuum from the brand. But the older Gen5Detect still holds up against the V16—and will cost you much less. Ultimately, the V16 Piston Animal is the vacuum to get if you really want the add-ons. But if you just want a great Dyson vacuum, there are plenty of cheaper options.

New Vac on the Block

The Dyson V16 Piston Animal (and its Submarine variant, the model I'm testing) arrives five years after the previous model in its line, the V15 Detect. The V16’s “Animal” designation—a term long associated with Dyson—refers to the Piston’s specialized hair-screw attachment for cleaning pet hair. Its biggest change, though, is its new All Floor Cones Sense cleaner head that adapts to different types of flooring, responding in about a second when you switch from hard floors to carpet or a rug.

entries.title: 7-OH Users Are Stockpiling Ahead of a DEA Ban
entries.summary: The opioid-like compound, which is found in kratom, can cause brutal withdrawal symptoms and will soon be a controlled substance. Some users tell WIRED it has relieved their pain and anxiety.
entries.content:
A couple months after completing detox for alcohol in June 2023, Cam got into a brutal motorcycle accident.

The 36-year-old upstate New York resident woke up hospitalized in late September after a month in a coma. “I broke every rib, every vertebrae. My pelvis was completely shattered,” says Cam, who asked to be identified by his first name because he is discussing drug use. He needed a spinal fusion and was unable to return to his job in car parts manufacturing.

“I was in pain 24/7,” Cam says.

He needed serious painkillers, and he says the 15 milligrams of oxycodone a day he was prescribed wasn’t cutting it.

“I didn't sleep for months. I would literally scream in agony, like crying, screaming uncontrollably,” he says. (Dosing for opioids can vary greatly depending on a person’s tolerance and pain level, but 15 mg is not considered a high dose—and Cam notes he used to take “20 times that” when he struggled with addiction in the past.)

In early 2024, he says he was served an Instagram ad for a free sample of 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH—a potent compound found in kratom that activates a person’s opioid receptors. The pain relief was “right on par” with a higher dose of oxycodone, he says. While 7-OH is available in gas stations and smoke shops around the country, Cam has turned to buying it in bulk online, spending around $500 for an order that lasts him a month. It’s allowed him to be more active and do chores around the house, or even go for a car ride without being in pain.

But all that is in jeopardy now, as the Drug Enforcement Administration plans to place 7-OH onto Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act—the same category as heroin—along with similar compounds MGM-15 and MGM-16. The temporary ban, to take place August 5 at the earliest, will be in effect for two years, with the option to extend it for an additional year as the DEA works toward permanently scheduling the substances. Already, a dozen states have banned 7-OH.

“Given its pharmacological profile as an opioid agonist and high abuse potential, the marketing of 7-hydroxymitragynine products to consumers as botanical supplements constitute a significant public health risk,” reads the DEA’s notice of intent about the proposed ban. The Food and Drug Administration does not regulate “dietary supplements” for safety and efficacy before they hit the market.

Some people have gone broke after their 7-OH tolerances escalated, leading to higher doses—one user tells WIRED prior to quitting, he was spending $175 every four to five days, but felt so sick he stopped working, and eventually couldn’t pay rent.

The DEA notes that people are using the unregulated dietary supplements to self-medicate chronic pain. Cam acknowledges he’s doing just that—and he’s terrified of having the treatment taken away.

“They're fucking a lot of people,” he says of the DEA. “It's caused me so much anxiety.”

The DEA’s action comes amid a wider rift between the mainstream kratom industry, which says 7-OH should not be classified as kratom because it’s much more potent, and 7-OH proponents who say the drug is helpful to many people and can’t be separated from kratom.

In pursuing a federal ban on manufacturing, sales, and possession, the Trump administration has sided with the kratom lobby. Health and Human Services secretary Robert F. Kennedy called the 7-OH industry “sinister” at a press conference last July, claiming that the products are “marketed for children,” in part because they are sometimes sold as brightly colored gummies. Department of Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin has also supported a crackdown on 7-OH. As WIRED has previously reported, both Kennedy and Mullin have strong ties to the kratom industry. (HHS did not respond to a request for comment.)

Because kratom—a Southeast Asian plant that has analgesic properties—naturally contains only trace amounts of 7-OH, it will not meet the threshold of the DEA ban. However, some users of both “natural” kratom products and 7-OH have suffered from withdrawal symptoms after they’ve stopped taking the respective substances.

Cam says he’s “dependent” on 7-OH, as well as MGM-15, which he started using because it lasts longer. “It definitely feels like shit to come off of, like any other opiate,” he says. But he says it’s worth it for the quality of life the drugs have given back to him.

In addition to alcohol, Cam previously struggled with addictions to prescription opioids and heroin. He credits 7-OH with helping him stay off booze, but notes, “I can see that being a struggle again when I’m back to being in pain and miserable.” While he says he’s committed to not going back to using street opioids, he fears that will be the case for many 7-OH users once the ban kicks in, possibly leading to a spike in overdose deaths.

Reddit and Discord channels, including r/quitting7oh, which has 11,000 members, are filled with advice about how to taper off the drug. That includes what supplements or medications might help ease withdrawal symptoms like anxiety, insomnia, and chills.

Archie, a pharmacy student who asked to use a pseudonym to avoid professional repercussions, started using 7-OH in March to treat pain stemming from an abscess in his jaw.

“I think I was three weeks in when I realized that when I skipped a dose, I was going into severe withdrawal,” he says. He continued using 7-OH until the end of the semester, he says, because “I could not do anything without it. I couldn't think. I couldn't sit still. I would have been drenched in sweat.”

When he checked out the brand he’d been using on a third-party testing site, it had been given an F grade because it was stronger than advertised and contained MGM-15, which wasn’t listed on the label. MGM-15 can be derived from 7-OH and also functions as a potent synthetic opioid.

Once school was out, Archie checked himself into a detox center where he was given buprenorphine—an opioid used to help people with opioid addiction by staving off their cravings—in increasingly lower doses.

Petros Levounis, chair of the Department of Psychiatry at Rutgers New Jersey Medical School and chief of service at University Hospital, says he sees a handful of patients in the emergency room a month who are seeking help with either kratom or 7-OH withdrawal. He says it’s become more common, and that physicians have also become more aware of it as it’s become more popular; kratom has been marketed as a wellness product, and podcasters like Joe Rogan and Andrew Huberman have talked about the drug’s effects. Doctors use a similar detox protocol to opioid withdrawal, but “it's still quite a novel substance. We haven't fully wrapped our heads around how to treat it best.”

While Levounis doesn’t think a federal ban is a bad idea, he is also doubtful that it will have much impact.

In advance of the ban, some people who can afford it and don’t want to quit are stockpiling. One California-based 7-OH user tells WIRED the compound has eased her severe anxiety and jaw pain associated with temporomandibular joint disorders, while helping her stay off street drugs she’s used in the past like fentanyl. She says she has a “substantial amount” of 7-OH at home and is adding to it.

Several users tell WIRED they think 7-OH should be better regulated, with testing and clear labels that state it can be addictive. They also say it shouldn’t be sold at gas stations.

“How can a developed nation like the United States have products on the shelf that do not contain what the labeling states it contains, whether it be melatonin or whether it be 7-OH?” says Archie.

entries.title: An Extreme Solar Storm May Be Even More Devastating Than Previously Imagined
entries.summary: Scientists have long assumed that there’s an upper limit to the intensity of the solar winds that reach Earth. New research suggests there’s not—and the implications are alarming.
entries.content:
It's well known that a solar storm, depending on its level of intensity, can affect the functioning of electrical grids, navigation systems, or satellite communications. The problem is that it's unclear what would happen today if the intensity of a storm reached levels like those of the so-called Carrington Event in 1859, one of those extraordinarily rare phenomena that occur only once every thousand years. New research, though, suggests the impact might be even worse than scientists had thought.

Solar storms occur when the solar wind—a continuous stream of charged particles emitted by the sun—interacts with Earth's magnetosphere. During the Carrington Event, telegraph communications collapsed across half the world, and the northern lights were visible throughout North America as far south as Cuba. In today's world, strong solar storms can have wider-ranging effects and can even alter the upper atmosphere.

“Our planet’s magnetic field does a really great job of protecting us against many space weather effects and so they often just show up as glitches or beautiful aurora,” notes Maria Walach, a researcher at Lancaster University who collaborated on the study. “There are however extreme cases, where satellites unexpectedly fall back to Earth, or we lose communication and GPS signals.”

To estimate the intensity of the solar wind, researchers primarily use measurements taken by satellites located at the L1 Lagrange point, about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth. The problem is that those observations do not correspond exactly to the environment where the solar wind ultimately interacts with Earth's magnetic field. A variable amount of time passes between the two points, and the solar plasma also changes during its journey.

The authors argue that this uncertainty, far from being mere experimental noise, introduces a systematic bias into the analysis of the data.

Solar Statistics

The central point of the study lies in a well-known statistical phenomenon called regression toward the mean. In simple terms, when a measurement is extraordinarily high, the true value it is trying to represent is, on average, less extreme. This happens because random uncertainties can occasionally exaggerate an observation.

In the case of the solar wind, an exceptionally intense measurement made at L1 probably corresponds to a somewhat less intense solar wind by the time it reaches the region where it actually interacts with the magnetosphere. If scientists directly relate that extreme measurement to Earth's observed response, the effect will appear insignificant relative to such a large stimulus. Repeated thousands of times, this effect creates the false impression that the magnetosphere stops responding as the intensity of the solar wind increases.

What has happened is that, for years, scientists have believed that there is a natural limit to the intensity with which Earth responds to the most extreme solar storms. According to that idea, when the solar wind reaches very high values, Earth's magnetic field stops reacting proportionally, and its response enters a kind of “saturation.” However, this new study suggests that perhaps that limit never existed. What appeared to be a physical phenomenon could, in reality, be an illusion caused by the way the measurements are analyzed.

To test this hypothesis, the researchers developed a statistical model that incorporates the main sources of uncertainty: variations in the time it takes the solar wind to reach Earth and the random changes it undergoes during that journey. The model reproduces with remarkable accuracy the same “saturation” curve observed in more than 25 years of data, without the need to invoke any physical mechanism limiting Earth's response.

They then applied a technique known as regression calibration, which mathematically corrects the bias introduced by measurement uncertainties. After that correction, the supposed saturation almost completely disappears. The relationship between solar wind intensity and the geomagnetic response becomes essentially linear again, at least within the range for which sufficient recorded observations exist—more than a million of them, in fact.

No Limit

What are the consequences of these results, as published in the journal Nature? If Earth's response continues to grow proportionally during catastrophic events, an extreme solar storm such as the Carrington Event could be considerably more dangerous than previously thought. The authors estimate that, for very high solar wind values, the geomagnetic impact could be approximately twice that calculated by traditional models.

“If there is no upper limit to our planet’s response to the solar wind, modeling for extreme cases needs to take this into account and we should be vigilant of space weather effects.” said Walach in the press release. “Fortunately, these very extreme cases are rare, but this also means we have limited data to work with and only time will tell what happens at the very extreme, one-in-a-thousand-year kind of event.”

Indeed, the study acknowledges that limitation: There are still very few records of the most extreme episodes. For that reason, the researchers do not claim that saturation is impossible. Rather, they argue that the available data do not provide convincing statistical evidence for its existence.
